hints: Think about what happens to the average energy of the same number of $\text{H}_2$ molecules when heated, and what this means for the total area under the curve.
Recall how the peak height and peak position change when the spread of energies increases, and where the new curve must cross the old one.
walkthrough:
Keep the starting point and total area fixed**
Picture the same sample of $\text{H}_2$ molecules, just hotter. You still start at the origin because no molecules have zero energy. The total number of molecules has not changed, so the total area under your new curve must stay the same as the original.

Spread the energies to the right**
At higher temperature the average energy increases and many more molecules have high energy. The distribution spreads out. To keep the same area while spreading out, the peak must drop down and move to the right toward higher energy.

Draw the single crossover**
Your new curve starts at the origin, stays below the original peak, then crosses the original curve once on the high energy side to the right of the original peak, and then stays above the original curve out toward high energy with a long tail.

Final answer: New curve starts at origin.
Peak is lower than original peak and shifted to the right (higher energy).
New curve crosses original curve once only, to the right of the original peak.

hints: Focus on the area under the Boltzmann curve to the right of $E_A$ and how it changes when temperature rises.
Link the energy requirement for reaction to the idea of collisions between $\text{H}_2$ and $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}$ that actually lead to products.
walkthrough:
See what $E_A$ really means on the graph**
Only molecules to the right of the $E_A$ line have enough energy to react on collision. That small tail area is the fraction that can be successful. Think of $E_A$ as the minimum energy barrier.

Grow that successful fraction by heating**
When you heat the sample the whole distribution shifts right and flattens. A much larger proportion of molecules now lies beyond $E_A$. It is not just that collisions are more frequent, the key point is that far more collisions have $E \ge E_A$.

Turn more successful collisions into faster rate**
Rate depends on frequency of successful collisions, meaning collisions with correct orientation and energy $\ge E_A$. Because that frequency rises sharply, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}(\text{l}) + \text{H}_2(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_{14}(\text{l})$ goes faster.

Final answer: A greater proportion of $\text{H}_2$ molecules have energy greater than or equal to $E_A$.
There is an increase in frequency of successful collisions between $\text{H}_2$ and $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}$ molecules, so rate increases.

hints: Recall the general role of a substance that speeds up hydrogenation of an alkene but is unchanged at the end.
walkthrough:
Name the role of nickel**
Nickel speeds up the addition of $\text{H}_2$ to the $\text{C=C}$ in $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}$ without being used up itself. That is exactly the definition of a catalyst, here a heterogeneous catalyst for hydrogenation.
Final answer: Nickel acts as a catalyst (for reaction 1).

hints: Think about whether a catalyst changes the molecular energies at temperature $T$ or changes the energy barrier they need to overcome.
walkthrough:
Leave the curve alone, move the barrier**
At the same temperature $T$ the distribution of $\text{H}_2$ energies does not change, so do not redraw the curve. A catalyst provides an alternative route of lower activation energy.

Show the lower barrier**
Draw a second dashed $E_A$ line to the left of the original $E_A$, at lower energy. A larger area now lies to the right of this new $E_A$, which is why the catalysed rate is greater.
Final answer: Mark a new $E_A$ line for the nickel catalysed route to the left of (at lower energy than) the original $E_A$.

hints: Start by remembering that this principle only applies when a reversible reaction is already at dynamic equilibrium and then disturbed.
Think about the direction the equilibrium position shifts in terms of opposing or minimising the imposed change.
walkthrough:
Set the scene of a balanced system**
Imagine a reversible reaction where forward and reverse rates are equal. The system is settled at dynamic equilibrium. Now you disturb it by changing concentration, pressure or temperature.

State the opposing response**
The system responds by shifting the equilibrium position in the direction that tries to undo that change. That shift to minimise the effect of the change is Le Chatelier's principle.
Final answer: If a change is made to a system in dynamic equilibrium, the position of equilibrium moves to minimise the change.

hints: Compare the yield of $\text{Z}$ at 300 K and 350 K at the same pressure to decide whether heating favours the forward or reverse reaction.
Look at how yield of $\text{Z}$ changes as pressure rises and relate this to the total gaseous moles on each side, $(a+b)$ versus $c$.
walkthrough:
Use temperature to find the enthalpy sign**
Pick any pressure, for example 200 atm, on Fig. 3.3. Yield of $\text{Z}$ is higher at 300 K than at 350 K. Raising temperature lowers the yield, so equilibrium shifts left toward $\text{X}$ and $\text{Y}$. By Le Chatelier, increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction, so the reverse is endothermic and the forward reaction $a\text{X}(\text{g}) + b\text{Y}(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons c\text{Z}(\text{g})$ must be exothermic.

Use pressure to compare moles of gas**
On both curves, yield of $\text{Z}$ rises as pressure rises. Increasing pressure shifts equilibrium toward the side with fewer gaseous moles to reduce pressure. Since high pressure favours $\text{Z}$, the product side has fewer moles, so $(a+b) > c$.

Final answer: Forward reaction is exothermic.
$(a+b) > c$, there are fewer moles of gas on the product side.
